fin-unit-economics-cost-per-x.core: Unit economics replaces 'how much do we spend?' with 'what does each unit of value cost?'. Pick units at the right level, calculate them from allocated cost and business (or proxy) counts, connect them to margins, and watch for diseconomies of scale.

first_principles.problem: Total spend alone causes panic or complacency without saying anything about efficiency.

analogy.title: Fuel efficiency for a delivery fleet
analogy.story: Total fuel spend grows with deliveries; what matters is cost per delivery, and whether bigger routes make it worse.
analogy.breaks: Unit metrics need good allocation, so tagging comes first.

example.title: A quarterly FinOps review
example.outcome: cloud cost is managed as a business metric.

check.q: What's the core formula of unit economics?
check.a: Allocated cloud cost divided by units of business output.

fin-cloud-strategy-ris-savings-plans-spo.core: Paying less means matching each workload to its pricing model: commit the stable baseline (Savings Plans, RIs where needed), keep variable usage on-demand, run interruptible work on spot, and at scale negotiate enterprise agreements that marketplace spend can draw down.

first_principles.problem: Defaulting to on-demand overpays massively for predictable workloads.
truths: Usage has stable and variable parts.
Commitments carry risk if usage changes.

analogy.title: Housing strategy for a growing company
analogy.story: Lease offices for core staff (commitments), rent day desks for peaks (on-demand), use discounted unused rooms for flexible teams (spot), and sign a portfolio deal with the landlord (EDP).
analogy.breaks: Commitments reduce agility. Keep some headroom for change.

example.title: An optimised purchasing portfolio

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Nearly half the bill saved with no engineering changes.

example.outcome: every dollar is spent at the best price for its workload.

check.a: The overall percentage saved versus on-demand pricing across all commitments, spot and discounts.

fin-allocation-showback-chargeback-taggi.core: Allocation answers 'who ate the pie?': consistent, enforced tags attribute direct costs, fair drivers split shared costs, showback and chargeback build accountability, and anomaly detection plus budgets catch and prevent overruns.

first_principles.problem: A single, unattributed bill means no ownership and no optimisation.
truths: Detection and prevention complement each other.

analogy.title: Splitting a giant group dinner
analogy.story: Itemised orders (tags), rules for ordering (policies), splitting the shared starters fairly (shared allocation), each table paying its share (chargeback), and a waiter warning when you approach the limit (budgets).
analogy.breaks: Allocation never reaches 100%, so manage the unallocated remainder openly.

example.title: An allocation programme

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: 95% of spend is attributed, and teams act on it.

example.outcome: cloud cost has owners who manage it.

check.q: What's the difference between anomaly detection and budgets?
check.a: Anomaly detection reacts to unexpected spend patterns; budgets set proactive limits and alerts in advance.

fin-greenops-carbon-aware-sci.core: GreenOps treats the cloud as physical infrastructure: emissions depend on grid carbon intensity (where and when you run), carbon-aware scheduling shifts flexible work to cleaner times and places, efficient hardware and utilisation cut energy per task, and SCI measures progress per unit of software output.

first_principles.problem: Software emissions are invisible, unmeasured and unmanaged.
truths: Electricity varies in carbon by region and hour.

analogy.title: Running a household sustainably
analogy.story: Run appliances when solar is plentiful, buy efficient ones, turn off what's unused, and track energy per task.
analogy.breaks: Carbon is one constraint among many: latency, cost, residency and reliability still matter.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Greener and cheaper at the same time.

check.q: Name the two main GreenOps levers for a workload.
check.a: Carbon-aware shifting (when and where it runs) and efficiency (less energy for the same work).

fin-financial-engineering-capex-opex.core: Financial engineering connects cloud decisions to accounting: CAPEX vs OPEX, depreciation and amortisation spreading asset costs, the EBITDA trap where cloud OPEX lowers a key valuation metric, capitalising eligible engineering labour, and a combined model of cash, P&L and unit economics.

first_principles.problem: Engineers and finance evaluate the same decision with incompatible metrics.
truths: Eligible development work can be capitalised.

analogy.title: Translating between two languages
analogy.story: Engineers speak 'latency and agility', finance speaks 'EBITDA and depreciation'. A good model is the dictionary.
analogy.breaks: Accounting standards vary, so always involve finance professionals.

check.q: What accounting lever can offset cloud's EBITDA impact?
check.a: Capitalising eligible engineering labour as an intangible asset that is amortised below EBITDA.

fin-contract-strategy-edp-ppa.core: At enterprise scale the contract is a FinOps lever: EDPs trade committed total spend for bill-wide discounts, PPAs price dominant services custom, leverage comes from commitment, growth, marketing and competition, marketplace purchases draw down commitments, and contracts are managed continuously.

first_principles.problem: Paying list price at scale leaves millions on the table.
derivation: Use an **EDP** for the base discount.

analogy.title: A procurement team buying wholesale
analogy.story: Volume contracts, special rates for key goods, negotiating at the supplier's quarter-end and tracking every contract year-round.
analogy.breaks: Over-commitment and lock-in are the main risks, so keep headroom and alternatives.

example.title: A complete contract strategy
example.outcome: spend is bought on the best possible terms.

check.q: What's the main risk of an EDP?
check.a: Committing to more than you end up using, which means paying for the shortfall.

fin-forecasting-models-monte-carlo-cogs.core: Cloud forecasting embraces elasticity: decompose historical time series for trend and seasonality, simulate uncertain drivers with Monte Carlo to get P50/P90 ranges, interpret budget variance as volume vs efficiency, and drive COGS-reduction programmes measured in margin.

first_principles.problem: Static spreadsheet forecasts and fixed budgets misread elastic cloud spend.

analogy.title: Weather and harvest planning for a farm
analogy.story: Use historical seasons, run scenarios for rain, budget by yield, and aim for a lower cost per bushel.
analogy.breaks: Models must be refreshed often, because the cloud changes quickly.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Finance trusts the numbers, and margin improves.

check.q: What combination gives a robust cloud forecast?
check.a: A time-series baseline for patterns plus Monte Carlo simulation of uncertain drivers.

fin-architectural-finops-storage-network.core: Architectural FinOps designs cost in: treat cost as a design requirement, match data to storage tiers and automate transitions with lifecycle policies, and design network topology to avoid the hidden tolls of cross-AZ, cross-region, NAT and egress transfer.

first_principles.problem: Reactive cost fixes can't undo expensive architecture without costly refactors.

analogy.title: Planning a city for efficiency
analogy.story: Zone warehouses by use (tiers), schedule moves to storage (lifecycle) and place roads to avoid tolls (topology).
analogy.breaks: Cost optimisations must not undermine resilience or performance SLOs.

example.title: Designing a new analytics platform
flow: Raw data → S3 with lifecycle to Glacier
Compute in same AZ as data

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Half the cost of the naive design.

check.q: Name two hidden network cost sources in AWS.
check.a: For example, cross-AZ data transfer and NAT gateway per-GB processing (also cross-region and internet egress).

fin-waste-reduction-zombies-rightsizing.core: Waste reduction attacks digital hoarding: find zombies and idle resources, rightsize to observed peaks, extend spot to tolerant stateful workloads, and keep it permanent with an automated detect-notify-remediate-prevent programme and a waste KPI.

first_principles.problem: 20–30% of cloud spend buys nothing, and it creeps back after every cleanup.

analogy.title: A well-run warehouse
analogy.story: Regular stock audits, right-sized shelving, flexible staffing and house rules that stop clutter from building up.
analogy.breaks: Always confirm before deleting, because some 'waste' is intentional standby capacity.

example.title: A quarter of waste work
example.outcome: lean infrastructure as the steady state.

check.q: What makes a waste-reduction effort sustainable?
check.a: Continuous automated detection, owner accountability, auto-remediation and preventive guardrails tracked by a KPI.

fin-cloud-free-tier-budgets.core: Learning the cloud safely takes layered defences: understand the free tier's exact limits, set budgets with actual and forecast alerts, enable anomaly detection for unusual patterns, and for teams use account isolation and SCPs that make expensive mistakes impossible.

first_principles.problem: Forgotten resources, misunderstood free tiers and leaked keys turn learning into big bills.
truths: Clouds bill until resources are deleted.

analogy.title: Teaching a teenager to drive
analogy.story: Explain the rules (free tier), a dashboard warning light (budgets), a parent watching (anomaly detection) and a speed limiter fitted to the car (SCPs).
analogy.breaks: No layer is perfect, so tear down lab resources after every session.

example.title: A safe training platform for a team

check.q: What are the three lines of defence against surprise cloud bills?
check.a: Budgets (alerts), cost anomaly detection, and SCPs with account isolation (prevention).

fin-saas-unit-economics-cost-per-tenant.core: SaaS unit economics asks what each customer costs to serve. Isolation architecture decides visibility, pooled systems need per-tenant metering and proportional allocation, tiers must be priced above cost with free tiers treated as CAC, and cost per tenant flows into margin, LTV and LTV:CAC.

first_principles.problem: Revenue growth hides customers and tiers that lose money.

analogy.title: Running a co-working space
analogy.story: Private offices are easy to bill, the shared floor needs usage tracking, membership tiers must cover their costs, and free day passes are marketing.
analogy.breaks: Precision has limits. Directionally correct and consistent is the goal.

example.title: A tenant profitability dashboard
example.outcome: every customer's profitability is visible and managed.

check.q: What's the key enabler of cost per tenant in pooled systems?
check.a: Instrumenting usage metrics with tenant IDs so shared costs can be allocated proportionally.

fin-cfm-finops-practitioner-phases.core: FinOps is cross-functional cloud financial management that cycles through Inform (visibility and allocation), Optimize (usage and rate levers) and Operate (governance, automation and culture), guided by six principles centred on collaboration, ownership and business value.

first_principles.problem: Decentralised, variable cloud spend escapes the traditional procurement controls.
truths: Gains only last if they're operationalised.

analogy.title: A household budget cycle
analogy.story: Track spending (inform), cut and renegotiate (optimize), build habits and review monthly (operate).
analogy.breaks: Maturity is a crawl–walk–run journey, so don't try everything at once.

check.q: In which FinOps phase does rate optimisation (commitments) happen?

fin-focus-open-spec-billing.core: FOCUS is the common language of cloud billing: a standard schema for accounts, services, resources, periods and quantities, clear cost metrics (list, billed, effective, contracted), explicit charge categories, and growing native support across providers.

first_principles.problem: Incompatible billing formats make multi-cloud analysis slow and error-prone.
truths: Different cost numbers answer different questions.
Standards reduce work as adoption grows.

analogy.title: A universal accounting standard
analogy.story: Like a common accounting standard, it lets anyone read any company's books.
analogy.breaks: It doesn't normalise product names or prices across providers.

example.title: A multi-cloud cost platform
example.outcome: billing data that speaks one language.

check.q: What does EffectiveCost represent in FOCUS?
check.a: The amortised cost of usage after applying discounts and commitments.

fin-s3-intelligent-tiering-math.core: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is maths, not magic: per-object monitoring fees versus per-GB savings give a break-even object size (~250 KB for IA savings), objects under 128 KB are excluded, and fleet-level inventory analysis with scoped rules decides where it pays.

first_principles.problem: Blanket enablement raises costs on small-object buckets.

analogy.title: Deciding which rooms get smart thermostats
analogy.story: Big rarely used rooms benefit; tiny closets don't justify the subscription.
analogy.breaks: Unpredictable access also justifies it to avoid retrieval fees, beyond the pure storage maths.

example.title: Optimising a data lake
example.outcome: storage tiering decisions backed by numbers.

check.q: What's the approximate break-even object size for S3-INT savings into the Infrequent tier?

fin-spot-orchestration-karpenter.core: Spot orchestration mixes an on-demand floor with diversified spot capacity, picks pools with price-capacity-optimised allocation, expresses the split with weighted Karpenter NodePools and topology spread, and treats the 2-minute warning as a routine graceful drain.

first_principles.problem: All-or-nothing spot strategies either overpay or risk outages.
truths: Diversified deep pools rarely all fail at once.

analogy.title: Staffing a restaurant with permanent staff and agency workers
analogy.story: Permanent staff guarantee service; agency workers from many agencies fill demand cheaply, and handovers are smooth when one leaves.
analogy.breaks: Strict singleton or latency-critical stateful workloads stay on on-demand.

example.title: A Karpenter-managed cluster

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Big savings with no availability impact.

example.outcome: spot as a dependable part of capacity.

check.q: Which Karpenter feature responds to spot interruption notices?
check.a: Interruption handling via an SQS queue receiving EC2 events, which cordons and drains the affected node.

fin-cloud-repatriation-exit-strategy.core: Cloud smart means placing each workload where it's most economical: rent (cloud) for elastic and new work, buy (colocation) for steady large workloads, accounting for full TCO, lessons like 37signals', egress and data gravity, and portable designs that keep exit options open.

first_principles.problem: Dogmatic 'cloud first' overpays for stable workloads, while naive exits underestimate the costs.
truths: Owned hardware needs high utilisation and ops skill.

analogy.title: Housing decisions over a lifetime
analogy.story: Rent while uncertain, buy when settled, and keep documents in order in case you need to move.
analogy.breaks: Operational maturity is the hidden requirement for owning infrastructure.

example.title: A hybrid strategy decision
example.outcome: infrastructure placement by economics and capability.

check.q: What are the two biggest hidden obstacles to leaving the cloud?
check.a: Egress fees for moving data out and data gravity (dependent services tied to the data).
